node.label: The languages of class debate
node.date_label: The Making 1963 · Languages of Class 1983 · ILWCH forum 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · Visions of the People 1991 · Vernon 1994 · “The End of Social History?” 1995 · Speaking for the People 1998 · ILWCH 57 2000 · The Future of Class in History 2007
node.description: Linked disputes over how experience, language, gender and social relations shape class formation and historical explanation. Thompson's preface (1963) made class a relationship, not a thing; Stedman Jones's Languages of Class (1983) set 'the linguistic cat among the social history pigeons' (Eley and Nield's words), while holding that 'how the two relate' — social and linguistic — 'must be rethought' (as quoted by Epstein). Foster, Gray, Epstein and Kirk answered (1985–87); Joan Scott asked that language and gender be taken seriously; Bryan Palmer replied (1987–90). Patrick Joyce set a 'family of populisms' against class (1991) and asked 'The End of Social History?' (1995); James Vernon asked who was afraid of the linguistic turn (1994); Jon Lawrence combined 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches (1998). Related and intersecting controversies developed across several regions: Rancière and Sewell in France, Wilentz and Katznelson in the US, Canning in Germany, Chakrabarty and Chandavarkar in India, James in Latin America, Cooper in Africa, Parr and Sangster in Canada. Eley and Nield asked for 'a truce in the Left's culture wars' (Cooper, 2000) and wrote its retrospective (2007).

strands.title: From experience to language: Thompson's preface to Languages of Class, 1963–83
strands.focus: Linked disputes over how experience, language and social relations shape class formation ran through the 1970s before the linguistic turn. Thompson's preface (1963) made class a historical relationship rather than a thing (the wording is on edge_924); Eley and Nield recalled 'the inspiration of Edward Thompson and Sheila Rowbotham' (2000, p. 24) and Cooper that Thompson 'wanted to show how the working class made itself, but never doubted that what was made was the working class' (2000, n. 11). From inside Marxism, Richard Johnson's 'Edward Thompson, Eugene Genovese, and Socialist-Humanist History' (1978) named a new 'culturalism', a word Eley and Nield recall adopting in 1980 (2007, preface); the Ruskin History Workshop of December 1979 was 'brought to a head' by The Poverty of Theory (Eley and Nield 2000, n. 46); Perry Anderson's Arguments within English Marxism (1980) found 'a disconcerting lack of objective coordinates as the narrative of class formation unfolds' (p. 33, as quoted by Bergquist 1990). Stedman Jones's 'The Language of Chartism' appeared in 1982 in The Chartist Experience, edited by Epstein and Dorothy Thompson, and in extended form as 'Rethinking Chartism' in Languages of Class (1983). The introduction set the programme: historians had set fragments of speech 'into direct relation to a putative experiential reality' (p. 21, as quoted by Foster); they should instead 'study the production of interest, identification, grievance and aspiration within political languages themselves' (p. 22, as quoted by Foster), without any 'simple prejudgement about the determining role of the "social"' (p. 7, as quoted by Epstein). Radicalism was 'a vocabulary of political exclusion' (p. 104, as quoted by Foster and Epstein), not the ideology of a class. He did not propose to replace a social interpretation with a linguistic one: 'rather it is how the two relate, that must be rethought' (p. 95, as quoted by Epstein, p. 202). He placed himself after Thompson, whose 'great achievement' had freed class consciousness from economic reduction, while rejecting the 'relatively direct relationship' Thompson assumed between social being and consciousness (p. 101, as quoted by Foster).
strands.works: Thompson, The Making of the English Working Class (1963), preface; Johnson, HWJ 6 (1978); Anderson, Arguments within English Marxism (1980); Stedman Jones, 'The Language of Chartism' (1982), Languages of Class (1983); the earlier essays reprinted there (1974, 1975)

strands.title: The first critics, 1985–87: from Foster to the ILWCH forum
strands.focus: The answers came from labour historians who accepted the attack on economic reductionism and refused its conclusion. John Foster (New Left Review, 1985), whose own Oldham study Stedman Jones had reviewed in 1975, called the theory 'undeveloped', set Volosinov's 'multi-accentuality' against Saussure, and read the book as 'an intellectual declassing of our understanding of language'. Robert Gray (Social History, 1986) found post-structuralist work on language 'a field of debate' rather than a method (p. 367, as quoted by Kirk). James Epstein (Labour/Le Travail, 1986) praised 'the most sustained and coherent descriptive analysis yet of formal Chartist ideology' but held that a public political language excludes symbolic action and that the fight over 'the people' was itself 'a form of class struggle'. Neville Kirk (IRSH, 1987) gave 'full support' to the opposition to reductionism and concluded that language and politics had been 'wrenched loose from their material determinations': 'an unconvincing idealism'. In International Labor and Working-Class History (1987) Joan Scott answered from the other side: labour historians 'reduce this important concept [language] to the study of "words"' (p. 1), and Stedman Jones had used theories of language 'in an essentially conservative manner' (as the journal's editors summarised her). Bryan Palmer answered her from the Halifax strikes of 1842, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism"' (p. 14); Christine Stansell sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss' (p. 24); Anson Rabinbach held that in Stedman Jones language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott's reply: 'class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (pp. 40–41). Cronin (1986) and Ellen Wood (1986) belong here but are unread.
strands.works: Foster, 'The Declassing of Language' (NLR 150, 1985); Gray (Social History, 1986); Epstein (Labour/Le Travail 18, 1986); Cronin (JSH, 1986); Kirk, 'In Defence of Class' (IRSH 32, 1987); Scott, 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', with Palmer, Stansell and Rabinbach, and 'A Reply to Criticism' (ILWCH 31–32, 1987)

strands.title: Visions of the people: populism against class, 1991–94
strands.focus: Joyce's Visions of the People (1991) held that 'the fixation with class' had denied historians 'sight of these other visions of the social order' in industrial England; its 'controlling narrative' concerned 'a righteous and dispossessed "people"' in a 'family of populisms', and popular Liberalism was 'about the union of the classes against class' (pp. 1, 56 ff., 329). Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) made popular constitutionalism the master narrative and found identities 'not done justice by Patrick Joyce's "family of populisms"' (p. 297, as quoted by Tilly); 'the invention of democracy in England was then a sham' (p. 336, as quoted by Tilly). Cannadine's review (NYRB, 1992; unread) asked, in Joyce's report of it, for 'a history of status', and his reply to Joyce's letter caricatured Joyce as reducing status to rhetoric and rejecting class as a grand concept (1993); Joyce answered that populism's flexibility enabled a history of social unities and differences. Tilly found in both 'softcore solipsism' by historians who 'remain captives of Thompson' (1994); Lawrence asked 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994); Kirk gave 'a materialist view' (1994); Vernon asked 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994; unread). Democratic Subjects (1994) carried Joyce's reading of class to narrative and the self.
strands.works: Joyce, Visions of the People (1991), Democratic Subjects (1994); Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994); Cannadine, 'Cutting Classes' (NYRB, 1992–93); Tilly, 'Softcore Solipsism' (1994); Lawrence (1994); Kirk (1994)

strands.title: The new political history, 1993–99
strands.focus: The Social History round on Stedman Jones (Mayfield and Thorne, 1992; Lawrence and Taylor's reply and Joyce's note, 1993; Mayfield and Thorne's reply, 1993; all unread beyond the 1992 abstract) passed into a new political history. Vernon's Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives in the political history of England's long nineteenth century'; Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' and the assumption of 'an increasing class-based electorate' (both as quoted by LoPatin); Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party', reconsidering the 'homogeneity' of the working class claimed by Hobsbawm and by Savage and Miles, and relocating popular politics in place and gender. Vernon reviewed it as 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed', written 'as though … by a schizophrenic' (1999); Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined and that scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'. Cannadine's Class in Britain (1998) offered three vernacular 'models' of class instead (as Willetts reports). The field strand political/new_political_history keeps each author's contribution.
strands.works: Mayfield and Thorne (1992; 1993); Lawrence and Taylor, 'The Poverty of Protest' (1993); Vernon, ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010); Cannadine, Class in Britain (1998)

strands.title: 'The end of social history?', 1995–96
strands.focus: Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (Social History, January 1995) put, in his own later summary, 'identity, modernity and structure' to the field as 'areas where the challenge of post-modernist thought was especially evident'. Eley and Nield's 'Starting Over' (October 1995; unread) defended 'the Marxist tradition in social history' as 'a plural discourse' and, Joyce said, equated 'my questioning of social history with contemporary neo-liberalism'; Joyce replied that it was not his purpose 'to "dismiss" or "bury" Marxism, class and social history' (1996, p. 96). Steinberg sought 'a commons between post-structuralism and the Thompsonian perspective' (1996; title). In 1995 Joyce's Oxford reader Class set Foucault's 'Governmentality' and Baudrillard's 'The End of the Social' beside Thompson, Stedman Jones and Scott, and Wahrman's Imagining the Middle Class traced the 'middle class' to political argument (publisher description). Eley and Nield recalled in 2007 that the 1980 proposals had been 'rapidly superseded by more extreme insistence on the autonomies of politics' and that the authors of those critiques 'turned increasingly to linguistic analysis and theories of discourse' (preface, p. vi).
strands.works: Joyce, 'The End of Social History?' (Social History 20, 1995), 'A Brief Reply to Eley and Nield' (1996), ed., Class (1995); Eley and Nield, 'Starting Over' (1995); Steinberg, 'Culturally Speaking' (1996); Wahrman, Imagining the Middle Class (1995)

strands.title: Gender, race and the making of class, 1986–2000
strands.focus: Eley and Nield dated gender's entry into ILWCH's field of vision to Scott's 1987 controversy (2000, p. 4); the debate developed alongside wider feminist revisions of class history. Carolyn Steedman's Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) set 'two working-class childhoods' in 'history, politics, psychoanalysis and feminism' (publisher description); Sonya Rose's Limited Livelihoods (1992) made gender pivotal in 'the massive reorganization of lives and livelihoods that accompanied industrial capitalism' (publisher description); Catherine Hall's White, Male and Middle Class (1992; metadata) and Anna Clark's The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) followed; Eley and Nield judged that 'the study of class has benefited powerfully from feminist revisions' (2000, p. 8). In Germany Canning, in Canada Parr and Sangster, in Latin America French and James (1997) carried gender into the class question (see the regional strands). David Roediger's The Wages of Whiteness (1991) asked how 'race and class came together' in the antebellum United States, treating white working-class racism as 'psychological and ideological' rather than only economic (publisher description); Cooper noted how wage earners could 'make claims in terms of a white working class, indeed a white, male working class' (2000, n. 10). Scott objected in 2000 that Eley and Nield spoke of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70).
strands.works: Steedman, Landscape for a Good Woman (1986); Rose, Limited Livelihoods (1992); Hall, White, Male and Middle Class (1992); Clark, The Struggle for the Breeches (1995); Roediger, The Wages of Whiteness (1991); Scott (1987; 2000); Eley and Nield (2000)

strands.title: Farewell to the working class? Retrospects and new bearings, 2000–16
strands.focus: In 2000 Eley and Nield asked 'Farewell to the Working Class?' (ILWCH 57): Stedman Jones had 'set the linguistic cat among the social history pigeons', Scott 'helped define the space where social historians might conduct such readings', and class 'discursively understood … is a better starting point' — yet 'We want to break this logic of disavowal' (pp. 7, 16). Scott answered that they 'foreclose other possibilities' and quipped 'Assent to Discourse' (p. 69); Cooper that their piece read 'like a plea for E. P. Thompson and Joan Scott to sit down together' but 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The Future of Class in History (2007) sought 'collaborative conversation across the polarized differences between social and cultural historians' (preface, p. vii). Joyce's ego-histoire related his 'interest in "the social"' to 'Irish and class identity' (2001); The Social in Question (2002) printed Latour's case for 'association' in place of 'the social'; The Rule of Freedom (2003) and The State of Freedom (2013) took Foucauldian governmentality and 'the new materialism' into the city and the state. In 'What Is the Social in Social History?' (2010) Joyce judged the 1990s debate partly 'vigorous and unproductive': 'heat exceeded light'. Gunn and Vernon's Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity (2011), from the conference for Joyce's retirement, returned to the Thompson–Anderson 'peculiarities' debate 'viewed through a "history of classes"'; Lawrence there argued for a 'conservative' modernity, and with Feldman recalled social history's 'retreat … as a "totalising" project'. Koditschek found The State of Freedom 'class-evacuated' (2014); Savage and Miles, the authors of 1994, reviewed it in symposium (2014; unread); Vernon took Joyce's 'secondary modern' title for his own essay (2016).
strands.works: Eley and Nield, 'Farewell to the Working Class?' with Cooper, Scott and the reply (ILWCH 57, 2000), The Future of Class in History (2007); Joyce, 'More Secondary Modern than Postmodern' (2001), ed., The Social in Question (2002), The Rule of Freedom (2003), 'What Is the Social in Social History?' (2010), The State of Freedom (2013); Gunn and Vernon, eds, The Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity in Imperial Britain (2011); Koditschek (2014); Vernon (2016)

strands.title: The United States: class formation and exceptionalism, 1984–93
strands.focus: The American round began three years before Scott's, in the same journal. Sean Wilentz argued, in the editors' summary, that 'the Euro-centric concept of a mass-based socialist or communist party as the appropriate index of class consciousness diverts attention from the ways in which workers in the United States have battled the system of wage labor' (ILWCH 26, 1984, p. v); Nick Salvatore replied that one must 'use carefully three related but quite different terms: class consciousness, class conflict and class formation' and that Wilentz had not 'travelled as far as he would wish from the position outlined by Louis Hartz' (pp. 26, 28); Michael Hanagan held that embedding in a country's political structure makes a difference (editors' remarks). Ira Katznelson and Aristide Zolberg's Working-Class Formation (1986) asked 'how class, rather than other social bonds, became central' to working people's 'ideologies, dispositions, and actions' across France, Germany and the United States, with chapters by Sewell, Perrot, Cottereau, Bridges, Shefter, Kocka and Nolan (publisher description); Eley and Nield note that it 'missed gender entirely' (2000, p. 4). Berlanstein's Rethinking Labor History (1993) carried Sewell's 'post-materialist rhetoric for labor history' (as cited by Sangster), answered in Frader's 'Dissent over Discourse' (1995; both unread).
strands.works: Wilentz, 'Against Exceptionalism', with Salvatore and Hanagan (ILWCH 26, 1984); Katznelson and Zolberg, eds, Working-Class Formation (1986); Berlanstein, ed., Rethinking Labor History (1993); Frader, 'Dissent over Discourse' (1995)

strands.title: Canada: materialist feminism and the discursive turn, 1990–2000
strands.focus: In Canada the debate arrived through Labour/Le Travail. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) held that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (p. xiii, as quoted by Callinicos 1992; the publisher: 'language is not life'); Mariana Valverde asked whether Scott 'exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make' (1990, p. 233); Joy Parr's The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) and 'Gender History and Historical Practice' (1995) deconstructed skill while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (Sangster 2000, p. 157). Joan Sangster's survey (2000) set 'the post-structuralist subject' against 'the Thompsonian subject whose consciousness emerged from the interplay of human agency with social, cultural and economic formations' (p. 158), set the Canadian feminists' retained 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' against 'the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott', and objected that when 'international writers' — Sewell, in Berlanstein's volume — suggest the economy is 'simply "constructed as material" (I'm sure the unemployed feel differently!), a more fundamental boundary is violated' (p. 157), tied 'the academic retreat from class' to 'the decline of the political and intellectual left' (p. 154), and concluded that 'easy accommodation, resting comfortably under one umbrella, is not possible' (p. 161). Tilly's 'Softcore Solipsism' (1994) appeared in the same journal. The existing strand cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000 covers the same ground from the Canadian field's side.
strands.works: Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Valverde (1990; 1995); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), 'Gender History and Historical Practice' (1995); Tilly (1994); Sangster, 'Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History' (2000); see cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000

strands.title: France: the language of labor and the myth of the artisan, 1980–89
strands.focus: William Sewell's Work and Revolution in France (1980) treated 'the "language of labor" in the broadest sense' and argued that 'The nineteenth-century labor movement was born in the craft workshop, not in the dark, satanic mill' (ch. 1 opening), with 1830 as 'the emergence of class consciousness' (ch. 9 title). Jacques Rancière's 'The Myth of the Artisan' (1983), the journal's first scholarly controversy, held that the skilled artisan's 'culture as a seminal force in the development of the working-class and socialist movement is exaggerated and stems from later internal myth-making' (editors' remarks); answered by Sewell and Christopher Johnson, he replied that 'the point at stake is the democratic meaning of worker militancy', that militants 'were sons of the French Revolution rather than of corporative struggle; Julien Sorel's brothers rather than Poor Richard's', and that social history 'in its new "cultural" approach, rests on a far too restrictive understanding of "social" struggle' (1984, pp. 42, 44, 45). William Reddy's Money and Liberty in Modern Europe (1987) found 'an increasingly poor fit' between class concepts 'and the reality they purport to explain' and proposed a new concept of exchange and authority (publisher description). Scott's 1988 chapter on Sewell is unread; in 2000 she returned to Rancière as 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield'.
strands.works: Sewell, Work and Revolution in France (1980); Rancière, 'The Myth of the Artisan' (ILWCH 24, 1983), with Sewell's and Johnson's responses, and 'A Reply' (1984); Reddy, The Rise of Market Culture (1984), Money and Liberty in Modern Europe (1987); Scott, Gender and the Politics of History (1988), ch. 5

strands.title: Germany: gender and the politics of class formation, 1989–97
strands.focus: German labour history met the debate through Alltagsgeschichte and gender. Geoff Eley's 'Labor History, Social History, Alltagsgeschichte' (JMH 1989), Alf Lüdtke's Eigen-Sinn (1993) and Jürgen Kocka's class-formation studies (Lohnarbeit und Klassenbildung, 1983; 'Traditionsbindung und Klassenbildung', 1986) are placed here by title and metadata only: none was read, and no argument is attributed to them. Kathleen Canning's 'Gender and the Politics of Class Formation' (AHR 1992; unread) and Languages of Labor and Gender (1996; contents read) 'disengaged class from the sovereignty of "objective" economic and social interests' while remaining 'Grounded in imaginative and meticulous studies of labor markets, workplace organization, job cultures, family and household dynamics' (Eley and Nield 2000, p. 8); a German reviewer saw it bringing 'poststrukturalistische Überlegungen zur Bedeutung von Sprache' into dialogue with structural history (Küster 2005). Stedman Jones restated his position in a Göttingen volume edited by Lüdtke (1997; unread; Eley and Nield n. 18, 20).
strands.works: Kocka (1983; 1986); Eley, JMH 61 (1989); Canning, AHR 97 (1992), 'The Man Transformed into a Maiden?' (ILWCH 49, 1996), Languages of Labor and Gender (1996); Lüdtke, Eigen-Sinn (1993); Stedman Jones in Lüdtke, ed. (1997); Welskopp (1998); Küster (2005)

strands.title: South Asia, Africa and Latin America: experience, culture and the colonial working class, 1988–2000
strands.focus: Eley and Nield wrote that their discussion 'could easily be carried into African, Latin-American, and South Asian contexts' (2000, n. 2). Dipesh Chakrabarty's Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) read Bengal's jute workers against 'an assumption regarding "culture" built into Marx's category of "capital"' and declared 'Culture, one might say, is the "unthought" of Indian Marxism' (pp. xi–xii; edge_916), separating his argument from Thompson's (p. 5 n. 9). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar's The Origins of Industrial Capitalism in India (1994) argued that both capital and labour were internally fragmented (publisher description); his 1997 essay examined Thompson and Indian history; its previously recorded quotations await re-verification. Imperial Power and Popular Politics (1998) 'reasserts the critical role of the working classes' (publisher description) and was reviewed by Chakrabarty (AHR 1999; unread). The ILWCH controversy of 1989 was Emilia Viotti da Costa's 'Experience versus Structures', citing Thompson's Ruskin paper and Scott's 1987 essay (reference list), with Barbara Weinstein replying 'What We Gain'. Daniel James's Resistance and Integration (1988) tried 'to avoid what the author calls "an essentialist notion of the working class"' and read Peronism through Williams's 'structure of feeling' (Bergquist 1990, pp. 309–10); Charles Bergquist warned that Brazilian historians were 'citing and quoting Thompson the way orthodox Marxists used to cite Marx and Lenin' and that 'Thompsonians … might well ponder how to implement his concept of class when so little is known about the class antagonists' (1990, pp. 192, 194). Frederick Cooper's retrospective on Thompson (Social History 1995; unread) preceded his answer to Eley and Nield: 'As in Thompson's England, much of the story is about people struggling not to be a working class'; 'The category-producing class is here to stay. So is the working class' (2000, pp. 62, 67).
strands.works: Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Chandavarkar, The Origins of Industrial Capitalism in India (1994), '"The Making of the Working Class"' (HWJ 43, 1997), Imperial Power and Popular Politics (1998); Viotti da Costa, with Weinstein (ILWCH 36, 1989); James, Resistance and Integration (1988), with French, eds, The Gendered Worlds of Latin American Women Workers (1997), Doña María's Story (2000); Bergquist (1990); Cooper, 'Work, Class and Empire' (1995), Decolonization and African Society (1996), 'Farewell to the Category-Producing Class?' (2000)

proposed_edges.relationship: Opens the debate: the 1982–83 Chartism essays and introduction, then 'The Determinist Fix' (1996) on the obstacles to the linguistic approach; Mayfield and Thorne (1992) and Lawrence and Taylor (1993) take his work as the case
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kirk 1987, pp. 2–3 (read): the revisionists' claim that workers were less motivated by class than the Thompsons and Hobsbawm held, with Stedman Jones (1982, 1983) the most fully argued case; Eley and Nield 2000, p. 7 (read): his Chartism essay 'originally set the linguistic cat among the social history pigeons'. Mayfield and Thorne take him as 'the case' of the linguistic turn (1992, abstract read); the 1996 title states a residual determinism as the obstacle to the linguistic approach (unread). proposed_edges.relationship: The first round answers him by name: Foster (1985) on an unargued Saussurean theory and 'declassed' language; Gray (1986) on post-structuralism as a field of debate; Epstein (1986) on symbolic action and contested signs; Kirk (1987) on 'an unconvincing idealism'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Foster read in full ('the book's very undeveloped theoretical introduction'; 'reductionism may take an idealist as well as economic form'; 'an intellectual declassing of our understanding of language'; 'The great problem is that these new assumptions are not argued'). Epstein read in full (pp. 199–204: 'the argument never really confronts the question of what constitutes Chartist "language"'; the fight over 'the people' is 'a form of class struggle'; 'seems to whisper gently "false consciousness, comrades"'). Kirk pp. 4–5 and 46–47 read ('wrenched loose from their material determinations'; 'an unconvincing idealism'). Gray known only through Kirk p. 4 (Gray p. 367 as quoted) and Eley and Nield 2000, p. 7. Scott's 1987 critique is drawn separately (joan_wallach_scott → gareth_stedman_jones). Each critic accepts the attack on economic reductionism; this arrow records their objections, not a verdict.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reopened the question after 1991: 'the fixation with class' had hidden 'other visions of the social order' (Visions of the People); 'The End of Social History?' (1995) put identity, modernity and structure to the field; he denied any purpose to 'bury' class (1996)
proposed_edges.map_label: Populism and the end of social history, 1991–96
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: introduction p. 1 of Visions (chapter opening read): 'Received wisdom has in fact become a dead weight, the fixation with class denying us sight of these other visions of the social order'; the 1996 reply, p. 96 (opening read): the 1995 article's 'points of substance … phrased in terms of identity, modernity and structure, as three areas where the challenge of post-modernist thought was especially evident', and 'It is not my purpose to "dismiss" or "bury" Marxism, class and social history'. The 1995 article itself is unread. Eley and Nield (2000, p. 16, read) 'welcome the critique of social explanation and the necessity of all the debates mobilized by Joyce and Stedman Jones'. Drafting addition built from agent B's evidence (§§A4, A9, P5).

proposed_edges.relationship: Tilly: 'shrill bravado', 'softcore solipsism' and a dismissal of democratic politics that his own evidence contradicts (1994); Lawrence asked 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994); Oddy found 'verbose but superficial' method in Hunger (2008); Craig doubted modernity as a singular condition (2016)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tilly 1994, read in full: 'Joyce fretfully and Vernon with shrill bravado' (p. 260); 'the Joyce-Vernon philosophical position obliterates any possibility of historical explanation' (p. 261); by Tilly's criteria Vernon's own evidence 'establishes a modest but real increase in democracy' (p. 268). Oddy (Reviews in History 695, read in full): 'the lack of methodological rigour which is evident in his verbose but superficial style'; Vernon's response read. Craig (2016, read) doubts modernity as a singular condition. Lawrence's 1994 review is known by its title only. Vernon's own answers are on his entry and on his 2009 response to Oddy.

proposed_edges.relationship: Carried the linguistic turn into political history: between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' (1993, as quoted by Tilly); asked 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994); gathered the new political history in Re-reading the Constitution (1996)
proposed_edges.map_label: The linguistic turn in political history, 1993–96
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Politics and the People pp. 107 and 336 as quoted by Tilly (1994, read in full; the book unread): 'this period witnessed a marked decline in people's ability to shape the political appeals available to them as the official political subject was redefined in the image of print'; 'The invention of democracy in England was then a sham'. The 1994 Social History article is unread; its title and subtitle answer Mayfield and Thorne (1992). Re-reading the Constitution: contents read. Eley and Nield (2000, p. 8, read): 'James Vernon eschews the normal ground of political history' for 'neglected traces like ballads, banners, cartoons, handbills, statues, architecture'. Drafting addition built from agent B's evidence (§§B1–B3, P5).

proposed_edges.relationship: Met the linguistic turn by combining it with social evidence: the reply with Taylor in the Stedman Jones round (1993), the critique of 'electoral sociology' (1997, as quoted by LoPatin), Speaking for the People against 'the rise of class politics' (1998), and the insistence that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches be combined (response posted 2010)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Speaking for the People, chapter openings read (via the chapter DOIs): 'Many of the historical certainties which once underpinned the notion of "the rise of class politics" have come into question over the last decade … the retreat from social explanation has by no means been as comprehensive as commentators sometimes suggest' (p. 41); the Cambridge description's challenge to 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party'. Lawrence's 2010 response to Vernon (read in full): combining 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches is necessary; scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'. The 1993 reply with Taylor is unread (title and metadata only); Party, State and Society known through LoPatin (1999, excerpt read). Drafting addition built from agent B's evidence (§§C1–C3, P5).

proposed_edges.relationship: Purdue: 'perhaps too wide in its scope' (2019); Goldthorpe questioned his re-analysis of the Affluent Worker files (2021–22). Vernon's 1999 review is drawn on its own arrow
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Purdue (THE, 2019, read): 'perhaps too wide in its scope', yet 'refreshingly optimistic and generally convincing'. Goldthorpe's objections (2021) are known only through the opening of Lawrence's 2022 TCBH reply: 'You did a great service to future scholarship by agreeing to archive the AWS files'. Vernon's 1999 review of Speaking for the People is drawn once, as james_vernon → jon_lawrence, and is not repeated here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Named answers: Cannadine, in Joyce's report of the unread review, asked for 'a history of status' and in reply caricatured Joyce's populism (1992–93); Tilly found 'softcore solipsism' and 'a doubt sandwich' (1994); Kirk 'a materialist view' (1994); Eley and Nield, in Joyce's report, equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1995); Koditschek a 'class-evacuated analytical approach' (2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The December 1992 review is unread; Joyce's letter (NYRB, 8 April 1993, read) reports that it ended by calling for 'a history of status' rather than 'a history of class' or 'a history of language', and answers that the categories of populism 'are important precisely for their plasticity not despite it' and open 'a history of social unities' that 'will at once be a history of difference'. Cannadine's reply (read) calls the letter 'disappointingly predictable' and caricatures Joyce's position — status 'merely a "rhetorical construction"', class 'rejected because it is a "grand concept"' — as Cannadine's summary of Joyce, not his own view of status or class. Tilly (1994, read in full): 'Joyce tortures himself on a rack of his own manufacture'; 'a doubt sandwich: a hearty slab of old-fashioned research between two layers of uncertainty' (pp. 263–265). Kirk 1994 by title only. Eley and Nield's 'Starting Over' (1995) is unread; the 'neo-liberalism' charge is Joyce's characterisation (1996, p. 96, read), as is their 'denial of creative conversations'; their 2000 essay (read) finds Democratic Subjects 'with no moorings to the densely contextualized studies of working-class life social historians have come to require' (p. 6). Koditschek (JBS 2014, read): 'class-evacuated analytical approach'; still 'Joyce's best, most innovative, and most insightful book—so far'. Mayfield and Thorne's 1993 reply to his note: metadata only. Joyce's own answers are on his entry.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson's preface, which made class a relationship rather than a thing (1963; the wording on edge_924), is the text every round argued over: Johnson's 'culturalism' (1978, as Eley and Nield recall it), Cooper's 'people struggling not to be a working class' (2000), Eley and Nield's 'Thompsonian rhetorics of experience' (2000)
proposed_edges.map_label: The Making as the debate's text, 1963–2007
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The preface's wording is carried by the existing atlas record and edge_924 (the earlier reading was made in a transcription whose route is now excluded; the source's link is corrected in this revision and no new quotation from the preface is made here). Later readers, read for 1.152: Eley and Nield 2000, p. 24 ('the inspiration of Edward Thompson and Sheila Rowbotham'), n. 46 (the controversies 'brought to a head in Edward P. Thompson's anti-Althusserian diatribe The Poverty of Theory'), n. 47 (cultural Marxism as the first of 'three moments'), reply pp. 82–83 ('the rethinking from Thompsonian and similar models began' with 'experience'); Cooper 2000, p. 62 and n. 11 (Thompson 'wanted to show how the working class made itself, but never doubted that what was made was the working class'); the 2007 preface, p. v (the 'culturalism' 'Inspired by the influence of Edward Thompson'). Thompson's own critique of economistic Marxism stays on edge_924.

proposed_edges.relationship: Opened the North American round (ILWCH 1987) by asking labour historians to take language and gender seriously, replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse' (1987), and answered the retrospective with 'The "Class" We Have Lost' (2000): questions that 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 1987, p. 1 (existing reading): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; labour historians 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"'. Reply, ILWCH 32, pp. 40–45 (existing reading, read in full): 'class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it'. 2000, pp. 69–72 (read in full for 1.152): 'Assent to Discourse' (p. 69); 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield (2000, p. 4): 'it was not really until 1987, with Joan Scott's scholarly controversy … that gender concerns … entered the field of vision' of the journal. Her critique of Stedman Jones is drawn separately; her critique of Eley and Nield stays on edge_1127.

proposed_edges.relationship: Answered Scott in the 1987 forum and the linguistic turn in Descent into Discourse (1990: 'Critical theory is no substitute for historical materialism; language is not life', in the publisher's words); Eley and Nield later called the book the reaction 'represented most viciously', a reader's judgement
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 1987, p. 14 (existing reading): 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism"'. Temple University Press page (read 2026-10-22; the book unread): 'Critical theory is no substitute for historical materialism; language is not life'; reliance on poststructuralism 'reifies discourse and sidesteps structures of oppression and resistance'. Callinicos (1992, read; existing record) quotes the book with pages: 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (p. xiii). Eley and Nield 2000, n. 46 (read): the reactions to Scott 'represented most viciously by Bryan D. Palmer's Descent into Discourse' — a hostile characterisation, recorded, not adopted. His critiques of Scott and of the linguistic turn are on edge_920 and edge_921; this arrow records his part in the debate.

proposed_edges.relationship: Named critics within the debate beyond Palmer and Valverde, whose arrows exist: Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (1987); Sangster's objection to 'the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (2000); Eley and Nield's charge of an 'ungenerous critique' that allows 'either discourse … or materialist social history' (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Scott's reply (ILWCH 32, p. 42, existing reading) reports Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject'; Stansell's own p. 24 (existing reading) sides with Scott on poststructuralism while holding that social analysis of real women's activities is needed (editors' remarks, read). Sangster 2000 (read in full), pp. 157–158: the Canadian feminists kept 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy', 'unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157; her 'constructed as material' objection on the same page is aimed at Sewell, in Berlanstein's volume, not at Scott); 'The post-structuralist subject thus stands in direct contrast to the Thompsonian subject'. Eley and Nield's reply (2000, p. 83, read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history'. Palmer's critique stays on edge_920 and Valverde's on edge_967; Downs (1993) is named in Scott's entry and not read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Her two-town study (1990) and 1995 essay deconstructed skill and treated 'portraits of experience' as 'interpretations, reclamations of sensations', while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (as read by Sangster, 2000)
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender, skill and experience in Canada, 1990–95
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Both Parr texts are unread (the existing Parr entry records the 1995 essay as known only through Iacovetta–Kealey and Sangster). Sangster 2000, read in full: the 'polar worlds of men's and women's work in small town Ontario' show 'the positive results of talking gender' (p. 151, citing The Gender of Breadwinners); Parr grouped with Tillotson, Mercedes Steedman and Creese as having 'deconstructed the notion of skill' while 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy are still in evidence, unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157); from the 1995 essay (p. 364) the sentence that portraits of experience 'were interpretations, reclamations of sensations which first had been organized, then claimed as experience' (p. 159, as quoted by Sangster). Moderate: a named reader's account.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) developed a related critique of labour-history categories through Bengal: 'Culture … is the "unthought" of Indian Marxism', an argument he distinguished from Thompson's; Chandavarkar's 1997 essay examined Thompson and Indian history (its previously recorded quotations await re-verification), Cooper used his 'abstract'/'real' labour distinction (2000), and Eley and Nield pointed to the South Asian exchange as where their discussion 'could easily be carried'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Preface and introduction read in the existing atlas record (edge_916): 'an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis; 'Culture … is the "unthought" of Indian Marxism' (p. xii); 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5 n. 9). Cooper 2000, n. 4 (read): 'Dipesh Chakrabarty['s] distinction [of] "abstract" labor from "real" labor', used to argue that 'the general and the specific both have their uses'. Eley and Nield 2000, n. 2 (read): their discussion 'could easily be carried into African, Latin-American, and South Asian contexts. See especially' Cooper 1995 and Chandavarkar 1997. Chandavarkar's 1997 essay is carried in the atlas's existing reading of HWJ 43 (edge_916); its previously recorded quotations await re-verification and are not repeated here.

proposed_edges.relationship: The debate questioned 'the sovereignty of the social': Stedman Jones 'Rightly castigating the unproblematized materialism of social explanation commonly assumed by social historians', Scott's discursively produced class, Joyce's 'end of social history?', and Eley and Nield's own concession that 'class discursively understood … is a better starting point' (2000)
proposed_edges.map_label: The sovereignty of the social questioned, 1983–2000
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Eley and Nield 2000, read in full: p. 7 ('Rightly castigating the unproblematized materialism of social explanation commonly assumed by social historians, Stedman Jones advanced an oversynthesized conception of public political language in its stead'); p. 8 ('there is no reason why "the social" should be held graspable as the effect of linguistic analysis alone in the way Joyce and Stedman Jones now seem to imply'); p. 16 ('we welcome the critique of social explanation and the necessity of all the debates mobilized by Joyce and Stedman Jones, which have rendered the sovereignty of the social so problematic'). Scott 2000, p. 71 (read): 'Structures come into being through discourse'. Joyce's 1995 question and his 2010 retrospect are on his entry. Distinct from edge_105 (language → social, citing Scott 1991) and from edge_1127 (Scott's answer to Eley and Nield).

proposed_edges.relationship: Labour history's categories — class consciousness, class formation, the artisan, 'experience' — were contested in ILWCH's scholarly controversies of 1983, 1984, 1987, 1989 and 2000 (Rancière, Wilentz, Scott, Viotti da Costa, Eley and Nield)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Editors' remarks ILWCH 24 (1983, read in full): the artisan's 'culture as a seminal force in the development of the working-class and socialist movement is exaggerated and stems from later internal myth-making' (summarising Rancière). Editors' remarks ILWCH 26 (1984, read in full): 'the Euro-centric concept of a mass-based socialist or communist party as the appropriate index of class consciousness' questioned (summarising Wilentz); Salvatore (read in full) on the three terms. Scott 1987, p. 1 (existing reading). Viotti da Costa 1989: title and reference list only. Eley and Nield 2000 (read in full): 'Farewell to the Working Class?' and the 'logic of disavowal' (p. 16). A critique of categories within the field, not a verdict on labour history; the field's own contributions stay on its strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Eley and Nield dated gender's entry into ILWCH's field of vision to Scott's 1987 controversy; the debate developed alongside wider feminist revisions of class history — Canning (1992–96), Rose (1992), Clark (1995), Parr and Sangster in Canada — from which, they wrote, 'the study of class has benefited powerfully' (2000)
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender and the making of class, 1987–2000
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Eley and Nield 2000, read in full: gender entered the journal's field of vision with Scott's 1987 controversy (p. 4); Katznelson–Zolberg 'notably missed gender entirely' (p. 4); Canning's work 'has disengaged class from the sovereignty of "objective" economic and social interests' (p. 8); 'the study of class has benefited powerfully from feminist revisions' (p. 8, n. 24 naming Clark, Rose, Baron, Frader and Rose). Sangster 2000 (read in full), pp. 151, 157, on Parr and the Canadian feminists. Rose: UC Press description only; Clark: existing record. The gender entry's own strands keep each author's work; this arrow records the debate's bearing on the field.

proposed_edges.relationship: Canadian debates included Palmer's materialist critique (1987–90), Valverde's sympathetic criticism of poststructuralist gender history (1990–95), Parr's gendered study of work (1990–95) and Sangster's materialist feminism (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sangster 2000, pp. 157–161 (read in full): the question 'whether we are simply replacing working-class history's failings concerning gender, with a linguistic approach that obscures class' (p. 157); Valverde cited for 'a certain logic carrying one from the (more generally accepted) deconstruction of notions of "male/female" skill to a complete deconstruction of class' (p. 158); 'Dismissing the "new" labour history as "mechanistic" marxism conflates diverse traditions of materialism' (p. 160 n. 121). Valverde 1990 (existing reading); Palmer's book through the Temple page and Callinicos. The existing strand cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000 covers Palmer, Morton and Sangster from the Canadian field's side; this arrow records the debate's entry into it.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chakrabarty's Bengal book carried the culture/experience question into Subaltern Studies; Chandavarkar's 1997 essay and Cooper's 2000 reply show the colonial rounds diverging from the British one
proposed_edges.map_label: The debate in colonial labour history, 1989–2000
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chakrabarty's preface (existing reading, edge_916 and the subaltern/labor strand); Cooper 2000, n. 4 (read) on the 'abstract'/'real' labour distinction; Eley and Nield 2000, n. 2 (read) pointing to Cooper 1995 and Chandavarkar 1997 as where the discussion 'could easily be carried'. Chandavarkar's 1997 essay is in the atlas's existing reading of HWJ 43; its previously recorded quotations await re-verification. Moderate: a comparison of two debates, not a claim that Subaltern Studies answered the British one.

proposed_edges.relationship: Cooper's retrospective on Thompson (1995) and his 2000 reply brought African labour history — 'people struggling not to be a working class' — into the debate's last round
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cooper 2000, read in full: 'As in Thompson's England, much of the story is about people struggling not to be a working class, struggles that were not without consequences' (p. 62); 'The Haitian revolution and controversies over slavery forced an empire-wide perspective into debates in Europe' (p. 63); n. 6 points to Decolonization and African Society (1996) 'for a fuller argument'. proposed_edges.relationship: Wilentz's American exceptionalism exchange (1984) and Katznelson's call to return to political history (1994) ran beside the British linguistic turn; Eley and Nield endorsed 'his desire to avoid binarisms' while keeping 'some basic disagreements' (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Editors' remarks, ILWCH 26 (1984, read in full): 'Twenty-some years ago the interests of historians of the working class shifted sharply away from parties and organizational leaders toward the actions, aspirations, and thinking of the working people themselves'; Hanagan: 'The ways in which working-class struggles have been embedded in a county's [sic] political structure do make a difference' (p. v). Salvatore (read in full) on 'the political history of exchange and property relations'. Eley and Nield 2000, p. 14 (read): 'we have some basic disagreements' with Katznelson's 'The "Bourgeois" Dimension' (1994) while endorsing 'his desire to avoid binarisms'; Katznelson's essay unread. The British new political history is drawn on the Vernon and Lawrence entries and the strand political/new_political_history. Moderate.

The Introduction's pp. 7, 12, 16–22 are carried only as quoted by Foster (1985), Epstein (1986) and Kirk (1987) until a library copy is read (evidence-stedman-jones-part2.md §3).
source_addenda.kirk_defence_class: Revision 1.152: pp. 2–5 (opening and statement of thesis) and 44–47 (state section and conclusion) read from the Cambridge Core PDF at the atlas's stored URL (scan OCRed locally; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-stedman-jones-part2.md §4): 'awful dread of economic reductionism leads not to materialism, but to an unsatisfactory idealism' (p. 5); language and politics 'wrenched loose from their material determinations'; 'an unconvincing idealism' (p. 47). Note 8 (p. 5): the criticisms of Edward Thompson in Languages of Class pp. 16–20 are 'brief but unmistakable'; Dorothy Thompson's work is not directly addressed.
